# Simulating genomic data

The exercises in this chapter will pick up from where we left of in the [chapter
on building demographic models](building-models.html) and use those foundations
to learn how to simulate genomic data from these models.








## Preparation

**To make sure we're all on the same page, save the following code in a new
script `slendr_scheduling.R`. You can see that this script is largely the
outcome of exercises in the previous chapter.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the script `slendr_scheduling.R`

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2) %>%
  resize(N = 100, time = 1800) %>%
  resize(N = 2000, time = 1000)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

:::







## Exercise 1: Simulating genomic data

Once we have compiled a _slendr_ model, we can simulate data from it. By
default, a simulation from a _slendr_ model always produces a
[tree-sequence](https://tskit.dev/tutorials/what_is.html) object (sometimes also
called ancestral recombination graph, ARG) as a result. We'll explore the
tree-sequence concept in a bit more detail later---for now we can treat it as a
black box which "magically" stores genomic variation of a set of individuals.

There are two simulation engines built into _slendr_ implemented by functions
`msprime()` and `slim()`. For traditional, neutral demographic models, the
`msprime()` engine is much more efficient, so we'll be using that.

::: aside

**Note:** The alternative engine implemented by the `slim()` function plays an
important role for spatial simulations and for simulations of natural selection
--- these are the primary two reasons why it's included in _slendr_ in the first
place.

:::

**Here's how you can simulate a tree sequence from a compiled _slendr_
`model`.** You will be seeing this kind of pattern over and over again, so it's
worth keeping it in mind any time you will want to simulate data from your
models.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts <- msprime(
  model,
  sequence_length = <length of the simulated genome [in bp]>,
  recombination_rate = <uniform recombination rate [in crossovers per bp per generation]>
)
```

::: aside

**Note:** For the time being, _slendr_ assumes a uniform recombination rate.

:::

---

**Simulate a tree sequence from your compiled `model` by adding the appropriate
`msprime()` command into the script `slendr_scheduling.R`, running it, then
storing the result in a variable `ts`. Set the parameters for this simulation as
`sequence_length = 1e6` and `recombination_rate = 1e-8`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

This command simulates a _tskit_ tree sequence from a _slendr_ model. Again,
note that we don't have to write any _msprime_ or _tskit_ code to implement the
simulation because _slendr_ does all the work for us!

```{r}
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)
```

:::

---

**Type out the simulated `ts` object in the console --- what do you see? Try to
relate some of the information in the printed summary to our quick overview
discussion of tree sequences. What's the difference between "samples" and
"individuals"? How many "trees" does the tree sequence have, and how many
"mutations" are stored in it? How many "edges" and "nodes"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Evaluating the `ts` variable in the R console should give you a summary of a
tree-sequence object with some lower-level technical details about the genomic
sequence which it encodes:

```{r}
ts
```

For instance, our tree sequence contains genomic information for
`{r} ts$num_individuals`
individuals, each of them diploid. This makes for
`{r} ts$num_samples`
samples in total, where a "sample" is a "node" in a tree
sequence representing one haplotype (i.e., one chromosome) of a simulated
individual. All other "nodes" (of which there are many, many more) represent
haplotypes of those recorded individuals for which we generally have
only a part of their genomic information---parts of ancestral sequences which made it
through recombination to some of the recorded samples.

And notice that there are no mutations! How can this be possible, if we
supposedly ran a genomic simulation? More on that later.

:::

---

From now on, and similarly to the symbol `model`, whenever we refer to `ts`, we
will be talking about some simulated tree-sequence object stored in an R
variable `ts`.










## Exercise 2: Referring to simulated individuals

If we want to compute population genomic statistics on simulated tree-sequence
data, we need a way to refer to individuals and populations. For this purpose,
_slendr_ provides three important functions: `ts_recorded()`, `ts_names()`, and
(occasionally also  useful) `ts_nodes()`. At the bare minimum, these functions
accept the tree sequence `ts` as their first argument (i.e., can be run such as
`ts_recorded(ts)`).

---

**Try answering these questions by running these three functions and inspecting
and comparing their outputs** (this is a good opportunity to refresh techniques
for munging tabular data introduced in the [_tidyverse_
chapter](tidy-basics.html)):

- How is the result of `ts_nodes()` different from `ts_recorded()`?

- What is the meaning of the `time` values in the tables produced by these two
functions? Are they the same in both?

- How many individuals in total are in the tree sequence based on these two
functions, and how many of them are in each population (this is indicated by the
`pop` column for each row)? Why do you get the numbers that you see (in the
context of the model which you programmed)?

- How does the output of `ts_names()` differ from the two table-producing
functions?



::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

- The function `ts_recorded()` gives us a small metadata table with recorded
individuals' names, populations, and times. This is very useful for whenever we
want to compute statistics for each individual or each population, study the
dynamics of those statistics as time-series (we'll see this later), etc.

**Crucially, each recorded individual receives a symbolic name: first its
population label, then a numerical suffix.**

```{r}
#| message: false
# this is the table of recorded individuals
ts_recorded(ts)
# this is how many individuals we recorded
ts_recorded(ts) %>% nrow

# this is how we can compute how many we have in each population
# -- these numbers are equal to the Ne programmed for each population,
#    meaning that we have the genome of everyone in the model (unrealistic!)
library(dplyr)
ts_recorded(ts) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally
```

- The function `ts_nodes()` gives us a much larger table of tree-sequence nodes,
which includes not only information about recorded individuals chromosomes (one
node, or chromosome, for each individual, meaning that we get two rows of the
table for each individual) but plenty of other metadata as well:

```{r}
# the entire table of metadata for every single node in the tree sequence
ts_nodes(ts)
# ... which is a lot of data compared to just recorded individuals!
ts_nodes(ts) %>% nrow

# here's a selection for a single individual (two rows because that
# individual is diploid)
ts_nodes(ts) %>% filter(name == "p1_42")
```

Additionally, the table also contains information about the recorded
individuals' ancestral haplotypes, i.e. individuals who lived in the
genealogical history of the recorded individuals, but whose complete genomic
information we no longer have (because they mostly likely passed only a subset
of their genomes to the individuals which we actually "sequenced" in the
simulation). Note that they, obviously, don't have any symbolic names attached
to them:

```{r}
ts_nodes(ts) %>% filter(time > 0)
```

- Finally (and most usefully in practice), `ts_names()` gives us individuals as
a plain vector of names, without any additional information.

```{r}
ts_names(ts) %>% head(10)
```

## Exercise 3: Scheduling recording events

We can see that our tree sequence contains a massive number of individuals. Too
many, in fact --- we recorded every single individual alive at the end of our
simulation
(`{r} ts$num_individuals`!)
, which is something we're unlikely to be ever lucky enough to have,
regardless of which species we study.

To get closer to the scale of the genomic data that we usually work with, **you
can restrict our simulation to "sequence" only a subset of individuals---using a
process I called "scheduling of recorded individuals" implemented by the
_slendr_ function `schedule_recording()`**. Simply speaking, this is a
functionality of _slendr_ which precisely defines which individuals will be
recorded in the tree sequence (while ignoring everyone else).

The function follows the structure in the following code chunk, representing
another very useful pattern worth keeping in mind going forward:

```{r}
#| eval: false
schedule <- schedule_recording(
  <compiled slendr model>,
  times = <times of recording>,
  list(<population object>, <number of samples to record>),
  [... etc. ... ]
)
```

Finally, you use this `schedule` object in a standard `msprime()` function call
by setting it as the argument of the same name (`schedule =`) like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

---

**To get an idea about what this function does in practice, modify the command
which simulates the `ts` object in your script `slendr_scheduling.R` according
to the snippet above, but include a schedule for recording 5 individuals from
each of the four populations. When you re-run the new simulation to get a new
`ts` object and type `ts` into your console, do you see a change? Again, use
your knowledge of `ts_recorded()` and some _dplyr_ table processing function to
inspect the set of recorded individuals.**

**Hint:** To make this easier to see, maybe keep the original simulation command
in your script (the one without the `schedule`) but modify it to create a
variable `ts_big` instead before you create the new `ts` object.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

We define our recording schedule like this:

```{r}
schedule <- schedule_recording(
  model,
  times = 0,
  list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 5), list(p4, 5)
)
```

After this, we use it in a new simulation:

```{r}
# original simulation command (note the missing schedule)
ts_big <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)

# new tree-sequence recording (with the schedule)
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

When we type the two tree-sequence variables in the R console, we see that the
new tree sequence is much smaller (not just the number of individuals, but also
its memory footprint visible as "Total Size"):

```{r}
ts
ts_big

ts_recorded(ts)
ts_recorded(ts_big)

ts_recorded(ts) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally
ts_recorded(ts_big) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally
```

:::

::: aside

**Note:** In order to make the recording of smaller number of individuals from a
(potentially huge) number of population easier, `schedule_recording()` supports
a shortcut of `list("all", <number>)` which records the given number of
individuals from every population in the model at the given time.

:::











## Exercise 4: Complex recording schedules

What if we need to simulate different number of individuals from different
populations at specific times instead of individuals from every population at
one time? Doing this with a single call to `schedule_recording()` is not
possible. Luckily, multiple schedules can be easily combined together into a
single sampling schedule. Let's see how to do this.

---

**Type the `schedule` variable in your R console. What do you see? Can you guess
why did I say that multiple schedules can be easily combined? And how could we
combine them?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

The output of any `schedule_recording()` function is a plain old data frame! It
contains information we used in the `schedule_recording()` call (population
names, times, etc.), plus a bunch more additional data which is currently
irrelevant. For instance, notice the `time`, `pop`, and `n` columns below:

```{r}
schedule
```

Normally we don't ever have to look at this data (unless something goes wrong
with the sampling and troubleshooting _slendr_ itself is needed), but knowing
the format of the schedule means we can easily combine multiple schedules using
standard functions such as `rbind()` (included in base R).

:::

---

In the following chapters, we will be working on implementing many real-world
scenarios from widely established research in population genomics, particularly
those from the field of ancient DNA. Naturally, in cases like this, we need to
be able to simulate sequences of "ancient" individuals as well as various
"present-day" reference panels.

In preparation for these complex exercises, **implement the recording schedule
summarized into the table below into your `slendr_scheduling.R`. You will have
to figure out how many individual schedules you'll have to create using
`schedule_recording()`, then bind them into a single `schedule` using the
function `rbind()` mentioned above. Then, simulate a tree sequence `ts` with
this new complex schedule, modifying your current solution script accordingly.**

| time (years ago) | population | # of individuals to record | interpretation
|-------------------|:-----------|--------------|----------------|
| 0                 | p1         | 1            | outgroup |
| 0                 | p2         | 1            | admixture source |
| from 5 k B.P., every 1 k years | p3       | 5            | time-series of ancient individuals |
| 0                 | p4         | 10           | panel of reference individuals |

**Hint:** To implement the recording of the ancient DNA time series, note that
you can provide a vector of numbers as the `times =` argument of
`schedule_recording()`. See the help page for `?schedule_recording` for more
information and to see a concrete example.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Inspecting the table above, it looks like we have effectively two groups of
recording events determined by the times indicated in the first column: one
group of individuals in the "present-day" (i.e., at time 0) and a time-series of
ancient individuals. So let's leverage that to create two recording schedules:
"modern" and "ancient":

- First scheduling of modern individuals:

```{r}
modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p2, 1), list(p4, 10))

```

- Then scheduling of ancient individuals:

```{r}
ancient_times <- seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000)
ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = ancient_times, list(p3, 5))
```

- Then we can create a single sampling schedule like this:

```{r}
schedule <- rbind(modern, ancient)
```

- Finally, we can use the `schedule` in our simulation just like we showed
above:

```{r}
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

Let's verify that we got the correct number of individuals:

```{r}
ts_recorded(ts) %>% group_by(pop, time) %>% tally
```

:::










## Exercise 5: Recording of named individuals

Sometimes, we don't just want to record a given set of "anonymous" individuals,
but we want to be able to work with unique, named individuals. This can be
especially helpful when we need to reconstruct a particular scenario in some
specific archaeological context (for instance, we want to work with some very
precious archaeological sample, such as the "Ust'Ishim hunter gatherer").

We can do so by calling `schedule_recording()` in a slightly modified way which
doesn't use the normal syntax `list(<population>, <number>)`, but instead uses
the format of `list(<population>, 1, "NameOfTheIndividual")`.

---

**Use this technique to modify your recording schedule (for instance, based on
combining two recording schedules called `modern` and `ancient`) to implement a
(third) unique recording event which will give the one representative individual
of the admixture source population the name `"source_ind"` and the outgroup
individual will be named `"outgroup_ind"`. Then create a new combined `schedule`
again, and verify that you got the newly named individuals in a new simulated
tree sequence `ts`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

We'll be more succinct now (see the full explanation to the `modern` and
`ancient` schedules in the solution to the previous exercise):

```{r}
outgroup <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1, "outgroup_ind"))
source   <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p2, 1, "source_ind"))
modern   <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p4, 10))
ancient  <- schedule_recording(model, times = seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000), list(p3, 5))

schedule <- rbind(outgroup, source, modern, ancient)
```

Now we can simulate a new tree sequence with more specifically named
individuals:

```{r}
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

And verify that we did everything correctly by inspecting the table of the
contents of the tree sequence:

```{r}
ts_recorded(ts) %>% print(n = Inf)
```

:::

---

**You may have noticed that `plot_model()` has a number of optional arguments.
One of them is called `schedule` and it accepts a sampling schedule (such as the
one you just created) as its input. Use your `model` and sampling `schedule` to
visualize your model.**

This functionality can be useful as an additional validation of your modeling
scripts, so always remember to use this for sanity checking your simulations
(after all, a picture can be worth more than <strike>thousand words</strike>
dozens of lines of code)!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Here's is the model on its own:

```{r}
plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

Here is the model with recording numbers overlaid on top:

```{r}
plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)
```

:::

::: aside

**Note:** As you've seen above, the visualization is often a bit wonky and
convoluted with overlapping elements, so don't be too frustrated if the results
of your `plot_model()` visualizations are not too pretty. The function has been
designed as a validation and troubleshooting tool, rather than a tool to create
publication-ready figures.

:::











## Catching up

If you want to just catch up to the point at which this section would conclude,
here is the version of our simulation script `slendr_scheduling.R` at the end of
the final exercise:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the script `slendr_scheduling.R`

```{r}
#| collapse: true
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 10000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 2000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 5000, parent = p2)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 2000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2100, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

outgroup <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1, "outgroup_ind"))
source<- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p2, 1, "source_ind"))
modern <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list(p1, 1), list(p4, 10))
ancient <- schedule_recording(model, times = seq(5000, 1000, by = -1000), list(p3, 5))

schedule <- rbind(outgroup, source, modern, ancient)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE, schedule = schedule)

ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule)
```

:::
